lines.text: Three men lived on this island.
When help finally arrived, all three were gone.
Two of them had taken their coats.
One of them... hadn't.
Why would a man walk out into a winter storm, on the edge of the Atlantic... in his shirtsleeves?
December, nineteen hundred.
Twenty miles west of the Isle of Lewis, in Scotland's Outer Hebrides, a cluster of rocks rises out of the Atlantic. The Flannan Isles.
On the largest, Eilean Mòr, stood a brand new lighthouse. It had been shining for barely a year.
lines.say: On the largest, Ellan More, stood a brand new lighthouse. It had been shining for barely a year.

lines.text: Three keepers lived there, keeping the light alive through the long winter nights.
James Ducat, the principal keeper.
Thomas Marshall, his assistant.
And Donald McArthur, a local man filling in for a keeper who was off sick.
On the night of December the fifteenth, a steamer called the Archtor passed the islands in heavy weather.
lines.say: On the night of December the fifteenth, a steamer called the Arktor passed the islands in heavy weather.

lines.text: Her crew looked for the light...
...and saw only darkness.
The Archtor reported it when she docked three days later. But the storms had closed in.
lines.say: The Arktor reported it when she docked three days later. But the storms had closed in.

lines.text: The relief boat, the Hesperus, couldn't sail. Day after day, the sea refused to let anyone through.
She finally reached the island at noon on the twenty-sixth of December. Eleven days after the light went out.
There was no flag on the flagstaff. No supply boxes waiting at the landing. No one came down to meet them.
Captain Harvie sounded the horn. He fired a flare into the sky.
Nothing answered.
Relief keeper Joseph Moore climbed the steps alone.
The gate was shut. The door was shut.
Inside, the fire was cold. The beds were empty.
And the clock on the wall... had stopped.
Yet nothing was out of place. The lamp had been cleaned and refilled, ready for another night.
The kitchen things were all clean. As Moore put it, they must have left some time after dinner.
The last entries on the log slate were from the fifteenth of December. Whatever happened... happened that day.
Then there were the coats.
Two sets of oilskins were gone. Ducat and Marshall had dressed for the storm.
But Donald McArthur's oilskins were still there.
Whatever pulled him outside... he didn't stop to put on his coat.
Days later, Superintendent Robert Muirhead searched the island's west landing.
Iron railings were bent and twisted. A rock weighing more than a ton had been torn loose.
A box of ropes, wedged in a crevice thirty-three metres above the sea, had been smashed, its ropes scattered.
Turf had been ripped away even higher, more than sixty metres up the cliff.
Muirhead wrote that the damage was difficult to believe... unless actually seen.
Over the years, the story grew darker.
Writers described an uneaten meal and an overturned chair. A logbook full of strange storms, weeping men and prayers, ending with the words: God is over all.
None of it was real. The meal and the chair came from a poem. The log entries were invented, years later.
The true record is quieter... and somehow, more haunting.
So what happened?
Muirhead believed that Ducat and Marshall went down to the west landing to secure that box of ropes.
McArthur, still inside, may have seen something from the window. Something enormous, rolling in from the Atlantic.
He ran out without his coat... perhaps to warn them.
One enormous wave. And all three were gone.
Their bodies were never found.
Today, the Flannan Isles light still shines. But since nineteen seventy-one, no keeper has lived there. It keeps its watch alone.
So what do you think happened on Eilean Mòr? Tell us in the comments.
lines.say: So what do you think happened on Ellan More? Tell us in the comments.

lines.text: Some stories should never be forgotten. This is the House of Owls.
Keep watching. Keep learning. And one day... you'll be one of us.
A member of the Owl Society.
